q: Who is the playwright of the play "The Book That Saved the Earth"?
e: "The Book That Saved the Earth" is a humorous science-fiction play written by Claire Boiko.

q: In which century is the opening scene of "The Book That Saved the Earth" (at the Museum of Ancient History) set?
e: The play opens in the twenty-fifth century at the Museum of Ancient History on Earth, where the Historian addresses the audience.

q: According to the Historian, what was the twentieth century often called?
e: The Historian explains that the twentieth century was called the "Era of the Book" because there were books about everything in those days.

q: In which year did the attempted Martian invasion of Earth take place in the play?
e: The Historian asks the audience if they have not heard about the Martian invasion of 2040, which was stopped by a single book.

q: Who was the ruler and Commander-in-Chief of Mars who planned to invade Earth?
e: The arrogant ruler of Mars and Commander-in-Chief of Mars Space Control was Great and Mighty Think-Tank.

q: What was the name of Think-Tank’s apprentice at Mars Space Control?
e: Apprentice Noodle was Think-Tank’s humble and intelligent assistant.

q: Who was the captain of the Martian Space Control Probe One crew that landed on Earth?
e: Captain Omega led the Martian crew on Earth, accompanied by Lieutenant Iota and Sergeant Oop.

q: Where on Earth did the Martian space probe crew land?
e: The Martian crew landed inside the Centerville Public Library on Earth.

q: What did Think-Tank initially think the books in the library were?
e: Think-Tank claimed that the books were actually sandwiches, which he believed were the main staple of the Earth diet.

q: Which member of the Martian crew actually bit off and chewed a corner of a book?
e: After Omega and Iota passed the "honour" down the rank, Sergeant Oop had to bite a corner of the book.

q: Which book of nursery rhymes frightened Think-Tank and ultimately saved the Earth?
e: The dusty old book of nursery rhymes titled "Mother Goose" frightened Think-Tank into calling off the invasion of Earth.

q: Who had replaced Think-Tank as the leader of Mars by the twenty-fifth century?
e: The Historian informs the audience that Think-Tank was replaced by the very clever Martian, the wise and wonderful Noodle.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: "Reena always ______ the truth."
e: "Always" indicates a habitual action, so the singular subject "Reena" takes the Simple Present singular verb "speaks".

q: Fill in the blank with the appropriate verb: "Babies ______ when they are hungry."
e: This expresses a general truth with the plural subject "Babies", so the plural Simple Present verb "cry" is correct.

q: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence: "Water ______ at 100°C."
e: Scientific facts are always stated in the Simple Present Tense; the uncountable singular subject "Water" takes "boils".

q: Complete the sentence with the correct verb form: "I ______ this watch last year."
e: "Last year" denotes a completed past time, requiring the Simple Past verb "bought".

q: Fill in the blank with the suitable verb form: "He ______ for Ranchi yesterday."
e: The past time marker "yesterday" requires the Simple Past Tense form "left".

q: "John is reading a novel." This sentence is an example of which tense?
e: The structure "is + V-ing" (is reading) indicates the Present Continuous Tense for an ongoing action.

q: "We have been playing for two hours." Identify the tense of this sentence.
e: The structure "have been + V-ing" accompanied by "for two hours" identifies the Present Perfect Continuous Tense.

q: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: "It ______ now."
e: The adverb "now" signals an action happening at the present moment, requiring "is raining".

q: Fill in the blank with the suitable modal: "______ God bless you!"
e: The modal "May" is used in optative sentences to express a wish, prayer, or blessing.

q: Select the appropriate modal to fill in the blank: "We ______ pay our taxes."
e: "Must" is used to express a strong duty, necessity, or legal obligation.

q: Fill in the blank with the right modal for polite permission: "______ I come in, Madam?"
e: "May" is the standard polite modal used to seek formal permission.

q: Choose the correct modal to show ability: "I ______ speak English fluently."
e: The modal "can" expresses present ability or capability.

q: Fill in the blank with a suitable modal: "______ you write a letter?"
e: "Can" is used in questions to ask whether someone has the ability to do something.

q: Choose the correct non-finite form: "______ is injurious to health."
e: As the subject of the sentence, the gerund (verb + -ing acting as a noun) "Smoking" is required.

q: Fill in the blank with the suitable non-finite verb: "She is too weak ______."
e: The structure "too + adjective" is followed by a to-infinitive ("to + base verb"), making "to walk" correct.

q: Which is the correct salutation in an informal letter to a friend named Kiran?
e: In an informal letter, both "Dear" and the friend’s proper name must begin with capital letters: "Dear Kiran,".

q: Which is the correct complimentary close in a formal application to the Headmaster?
e: School applications use "Yours obediently"—without an apostrophe in "Yours" and using the adverb "obediently".

q: After "To," in a formal school application, which capitalization and punctuation format is correct?
e: In a formal application, the official title uses title case capitalization: "The Headmaster,".

q: Which device did the Historian turn on to show the audience what happened in 2040?
e: The Historian turned on the historiscope to show the audience the events of 2040.

q: How are Think-Tank’s physical appearance and attire described in the play?
o: A small head and plain cotton clothes
A huge, egg-shaped head and a long robe decorated with stars and circles
Iron armour and a metal helmet
A red crown and a golden coat
e: According to the stage directions, Think-Tank has a huge, egg-shaped head and wears a long robe decorated with stars and circles.

q: How did Think-Tank refer to Earth and Earthlings?
o: A mighty planet and wise scientists
A ridiculous little planet and ugly Earthlings with tiny heads
e: Proud of his own giant head, Think-Tank called Earth "that ridiculous little planet" and humans "ugly Earthlings with their tiny heads".

q: By what time did Think-Tank want to put Earth under Mars’s "generous rulership"?
o: By the end of the week
e: Think-Tank boastfully announced that he intended to take over Earth "before lunch".

q: How many "peculiar items" (books) had Lieutenant Iota counted in the library?
e: Lieutenant Iota told Captain Omega that she had counted two thousand of those peculiar items in the room.

q: What did Sergeant Oop first guess the books in the library might be?
e: Sergeant Oop opened a book, put it on his head, and guessed that they might be hats in a haberdashery.

q: According to Noodle’s first polite suggestion, how did Earthlings use those "sandwiches" (books)?
o: As some sort of communication device
e: Noodle politely suggested that in surveyor films Earthlings did not eat them, but used them as a communication device.

q: Why did Think-Tank order Omega, Iota, and Oop to take chemical vitamins?
o: So they could lift heavy books
To protect themselves from Earth’s cold
To increase their intelligence so they could decipher the printed code
e: Think-Tank ordered them to swallow vitamins from the chemical department to increase their intelligence and decode the written lines.

q: Which nursery rhyme did Captain Omega read first after taking the vitamins?
e: Captain Omega first read the nursery rhyme "Mistress Mary, quite contrary, How does your garden grow?"

q: Which rhyme did Lieutenant Iota read aloud from "Mother Goose"?
e: Lieutenant Iota read "Hey diddle diddle! The cat and the fiddle, The cow jumped over the moon..."

q: The illustration of which rhyme terrified Think-Tank into believing it was a picture of himself?
e: When Sergeant Oop held up the large picture of Humpty Dumpty, Think-Tank screamed that the egg-shaped figure was himself.

q: To which star system did Think-Tank order the Martians to evacuate and flee?
e: Think-Tank ordered the evacuation of Mars and fled to Alpha Centauri, a hundred million miles away.

q: Select the correct verb to fill in the blank: "Bread and butter ______ my favourite breakfast."
e: "Bread and butter" represents a single combined dish here, so it takes the singular verb "is".

q: Fill in the blank with the right verb: "Honesty ______ the best policy."
e: Proverbs take the Simple Present Tense, and the singular abstract noun "Honesty" requires "is".

q: Complete the given sentence with the correct option: "Heena ______ from fever since last Sunday."
e: "Since last Sunday" indicates an action that started in the past and continues into the present, requiring "has been suffering".

q: Choose the correct tense form: "I ______ football for five years."
e: With the duration "for five years" and subject "I", Present Perfect Continuous "have been playing" is required.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct verb form: "I ______ when the lights went off."
e: An ongoing past action interrupted by a short past event ("when the lights went off") takes the Past Continuous "was reading".

q: Select the right verb form: "When we were taking lunch, the postman ______ at the door."
e: The interrupting action occurring while another action was in progress takes the Simple Past verb "knocked".

q: Fill in the blank with the correct modal: "I ______ run faster when I was a boy."
e: The modal "could" is used to express past ability ("when I was a boy").

q: Choose the correct modal to complete the sentence: "Work hard lest you ______ fail."
e: In standard English grammar, the conjunction "lest" is always followed by the modal "should".

q: Fill in the blank with the appropriate modal: "She worked hard so that she ______ pass."
e: Since the main verb "worked" is in the past tense, the purpose clause with "so that" takes the past modal "might".

q: Fill in the blank with the correct word: "He does not know ______ to drive a car."
e: To express knowing the method or skill of doing something, English uses the pattern "know + how + to-infinitive".

q: Choose the correct participle to complete the sentence: "A ______ chair is of no use."
e: The past participle "broken" acts as an adjective before "chair" to describe its damaged state.

q: Choose the correct passive voice for the sentence: "She helps me."
e: Simple Present active changes to "am/is/are + past participle", turning the object "me" into subject "I": "I am helped by her."

q: Select the correct passive voice of: "I know him."
o: He has been known by me.
e: In the passive voice, the verb "known" takes the preposition "to" rather than "by": "He is known to me."

q: Transform into indirect speech: The teacher said, "The sun rises in the east."
o: The teacher asked that the sun rises in the east.
The teacher said that the sun rises in the east.
The teacher said that the sun rose in the east.
The teacher told me that the sun rising in the east.
e: Because "the sun rises in the east" is a universal truth, its tense remains in the Simple Present in indirect speech.

q: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Please open the door."
o: He ordered me that open the door.
He asked me if I open the door.
He requested me to open the door.
He told me please open the door.
e: An imperative request with "Please" changes the reporting verb to "requested" followed by the to-infinitive ("to open").

q: Transform the sentence by removing "too": "She is too lazy to write."
o: She is very lazy to write.
She is so lazy that she could not write.
She is not lazy enough to write.
She is so lazy that she cannot write.
e: In the present tense, removing "too...to" uses the pattern "so + adjective + that + subject + cannot + base verb".

q: Choose the right word to complete the sign-off of an informal letter to a friend: "Your ______ friend"
e: Before the noun "friend", the adjective "loving" is required ("Your loving friend"), whereas "lovingly" is used only in "Yours lovingly".

q: Complete the formal leave application line: "I am therefore compelled to ______ myself from school for two days."
e: In a formal leave application, "absent myself from school" is the standard grammatical expression for staying away.

q: Why did Think-Tank force Noodle to repeat his salutation from the very beginning?
o: Because Noodle omitted the phrase "most powerful and intelligent creature in the whole universe"
Because Noodle had praised planet Earth
Because Noodle’s microphone was switched off
e: Think-Tank was deeply vain; when Noodle left out "most powerful and intelligent creature in the whole universe", Think-Tank made him recite the whole salutation again.

q: How did Noodle tactfully give correct ideas to Think-Tank without offending Think-Tank’s ego?
o: By defeating him in an open debate
By presenting them humbly as "insignificant" or "cloudy" data floating in his mind so Think-Tank could claim credit
By bluntly telling Think-Tank he was wrong
By calling scientists from other planets
e: Noodle framed every sensible clue as an "insignificant" or "cloudy" thought, allowing Think-Tank to adopt it proudly as his own.

q: Why did Captain Omega pass the "honour" of eating the sandwich to Lieutenant Iota, and Iota to Sergeant Oop?
o: Because Oop had been starving for days
Because the book was meant only for a sergeant
Because neither wanted to eat the strange object, so they pushed the task down the rank disguised as an honour
e: Neither Omega nor Iota wanted to eat the bizarre object, so they used military hierarchy to pass the risky task downward as an "honour".

q: How did Sergeant Oop describe the taste of the corner of the "Mother Goose" book he chewed?
o: Not delicious at all — as dry as Martian dust
e: Making terrible faces, Oop reported that it was not delicious at all and was "as dry as Martian dust".

q: Why did the rhyme "Mistress Mary, quite contrary" alarm Think-Tank?
o: He thought Earthlings had combined agriculture and mining to grow silver, cockle shells, and high explosives
He suspected Mary was a Martian spy
He was allergic to garden flowers
He thought Earth had run out of water
e: Taking "silver bells", "cockle shells", and "pretty maids" literally, Think-Tank concluded Earthlings could grow metals and high explosives.

q: What conclusion did Think-Tank draw about Earth’s domesticated animals after hearing "Hey Diddle Diddle"?
o: That Earth animals were weak and starving
That Earthlings had taught animals musical culture and space techniques and might launch an attack of millions of cows
That dogs and cats lived only in forests
That cows existed only in old stories
e: From the cat playing the fiddle, the dog laughing, and the cow jumping over the moon, Think-Tank inferred animals were trained in culture and space warfare.

q: Why did Think-Tank scream "It’s me!" upon seeing the picture of Humpty Dumpty?
o: Because Think-Tank’s name was printed on the picture
Because Humpty Dumpty was wearing a Martian uniform
Because Humpty Dumpty’s huge, egg-shaped head looked just like Think-Tank’s own "Great and Mighty Balloon Brain"
Because Sergeant Oop hinted that it was him
e: Seeing the giant egg-shaped Humpty Dumpty, Think-Tank immediately mistook it for his own "Great and Mighty Balloon Brain".

q: How did Think-Tank interpret the line "Humpty Dumpty had a great fall"?
o: That the autumn season (fall) was arriving on Earth
That the walls of Mars palace were weak
That Sergeant Oop was about to trip and fall
That Earthlings planned to capture Mars Central Control and overthrow Think-Tank himself
e: Think-Tank interpreted "had a great fall" as an Earth plot to invade Mars Central Control and capture him.

q: What is the irony in Think-Tank’s confident claim that "Sandwiches are the main staple of Earth diet"?
o: Despite claiming supreme intelligence, he foolishly mistook books in a library for edible food
Nobody on Earth actually ate food
Sandwiches were eaten only on Mars
The library actually stored real sandwiches
e: Despite boasting of unmatched wisdom, Think-Tank could not even distinguish between a book and a sandwich.

q: What positive cultural changes happened on Mars after Noodle replaced Think-Tank?
o: Martians destroyed all books on Mars
Earthlings taught them to read and set up a model library in the Martian capital of Marsopolis
Martians launched a second invasion of Earth
Both planets cut off all communication permanently
e: After making peace, Earthlings taught Martians how to read, explained books vs sandwiches, and established a model library in Marsopolis.

q: Even as friends of Earth in the 25th century, which single book can Martians never bring themselves to read?
o: A manual on rockets and missiles
e: The Historian chuckles that while Martians learned to read everything else, they can never bring themselves to read "Mother Goose".

q: Choose the correct verb to complete the sentence: "His brother along with his friends ______ leaving for the stadium."
e: When subjects are joined by "along with", the verb agrees with the first subject ("His brother"), which is singular, so "is" is correct.

q: Complete the sentence with the appropriate option: "Two-thirds of the students ______ present at the inaugural function."
e: With fractions like "Two-thirds of", the verb agrees with the noun following "of"; since "students" is plural, the plural verb "were" is used.

q: Choose the correct determiner: "______ community member was given a different set of equipment."
e: Both the noun "community member" and the verb "was" are singular, so only the singular distributive determiner "Each" fits.

q: Select the right quantifier to fill in the blank: "______ students attended the seminar today than yesterday."
e: Because "students" is a countable plural noun, the comparative quantifier "Fewer" is used instead of "Less".

q: Fill in the blank to form a correct third conditional: "______ he telephoned me, I would have visited his home."
e: In an inverted third conditional clause (replacing "If he had telephoned"), "Had" precedes the subject followed by the past participle.

q: Fill in the blank with the right tense form: "This July, you ______ in Japan for three years."
e: To indicate an action continuing up to a future point ("This July") over a duration ("for three years"), Future Perfect Continuous "will have been living" is used.

q: Choose the correct verb for this unreal wish: "I wish I ______ rich."
e: Unreal or hypothetical wishes after "I wish" take the subjunctive form "were" regardless of the subject.

q: Complete the sentence with the correct verb form: "Before the ambulance arrived, the injured passenger ______."
e: An action completed before another past event ("arrived") takes the Past Perfect Tense "had fainted".

q: Choose the correct passive voice for: "Who made this house?"
o: By who is this house made?
By whom was this house made?
e: A Simple Past active question beginning with "Who" changes in passive voice to "By whom + was + subject + past participle?".

q: Identify the correct passive voice of: "Mani is writing a letter."
o: A letter is being written by Mani.
A letter was written by Mani.
A letter is written by Mani.
e: Present Continuous ("is writing") takes "is/am/are + being + past participle" in the passive voice.

q: Choose the most appropriate passive voice of: "Someone stole my book."
o: My book is stolen by someone.
e: Simple Past active changes to "was/were + past participle", and vague agents like "someone" are omitted: "My book was stolen."

q: Select the correct passive voice for: "He teaches me English."
o: I was taught English by him.
I am taught English by her.
I am taught English by him.
He is taught English by me.
e: Turning the indirect object "me" into the subject "I" with Simple Present passive gives "I am taught English by him."

q: Choose the correct indirect speech for: Rani said to me, "Where are you going?"
o: Rani asked me where was I going.
Rani told me where are you going.
Rani said to me that where I was going.
Rani asked me where I was going.
e: In reported wh-questions, "that" is omitted and the clause uses declarative word order (subject before verb): "where I was going."

q: Report the question correctly: He said to me, "Will you help me?"
o: He asked me if I would help him.
He asked me that I would help him.
He said to me if I will help him.
He asked me would I help him.
e: Yes/No questions use "if/whether" in indirect speech, backshift "will" to "would", and keep subject-before-verb order.

q: Choose the correct indirect speech of: Raju said, "I was playing yesterday."
o: Raju said that he was playing yesterday.
Raju said that he had been playing the day before.
Raju told that he was playing the day before.
Raju said that he is playing the day before.
e: In reported speech, Past Continuous shifts to Past Perfect Continuous ("had been playing") and "yesterday" changes to "the day before".

q: Select the accurate indirect narration: Radha said to me, "I will help you today."
o: Radha told me that she will help me today.
Radha said me that I would help her that day.
Radha told me that she would help me that day.
Radha asked me if she would help me that day.
e: Reporting this statement changes "said to me" to "told me", "will" to "would", "you" to "me", and "today" to "that day".

q: Transform "Man is mortal." into a negative sentence without changing its meaning:
e: To change into a negative sentence while keeping the meaning identical, pair "not" with the antonym of "mortal": "Man is not immortal."

q: Convert the rhetorical question into an assertive sentence: "Who can control the wind?"
e: A rhetorical question starting with "Who" and a positive verb implies negation, transforming to "Nobody can control the wind."

q: Complete the formal letter excerpt with the right form: "Thank you for ______ my application. I look forward to working in your organization."
e: After the preposition "for", the gerund (verb + -ing) form "considering" must be used.

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

q:

o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

q:

Reason (R): By the 25th century, Think-Tank had been replaced by Wise and Wonderful Noodle.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

q:

q: What is the central satirical target of Claire Boiko’s play "The Book That Saved the Earth"?
o: Pompous, authoritarian leaders (like Think-Tank) whose vanity and half-baked guesses lead to their comical downfall
Ordinary librarians working in public libraries
Authors who compose nursery rhymes for children
e: The play satirizes pompous, authoritarian rulers who claim supreme intellect while making absurd blunders and panicking at harmless rhymes.

q: How is dramatic irony created during Scene 2 when Think-Tank analyses the books in the Centerville Public Library?
o: The audience also does not know what books are
The audience knows they are harmless books and nursery rhymes, while Think-Tank confidently treats them as sandwiches, spy devices, and military threats
Captain Omega reveals the truth to Think-Tank
Think-Tank secretly visits Earth to read the books
e: Dramatic irony arises because the audience knows the harmless truth about books while Think-Tank misreads them with pompous certainty.

q: How does the dynamic between Think-Tank and Noodle contrast genuine intelligence with false superiority?
o: Both make identical wrong guesses throughout the play
Think-Tank consistently makes wise decisions without Noodle’s help
Think-Tank boasts of a giant brain while blundering foolishly, whereas Noodle quietly supplies every sensible deduction masked as deference
e: Think-Tank embodies hollow vanity and bluster, while Noodle demonstrates real observation, tact, and practical intelligence.

q: Why is it ironic that "Mother Goose"—rather than scientific manuals or weapons—saved Earth from the 2040 Martian invasion?
o: Because no science books had ever been written on Earth
Because the rhymes secretly contained missile formulas
Because Martians always fell asleep on hearing poetry
Because harmless children’s rhymes achieved through Think-Tank’s paranoid misreading what rockets and missiles might not have
e: An old book of playful children’s rhymes defeated an entire alien invasion fleet solely because of the commander’s paranoid literalism.

q: What comic irony lies in Think-Tank’s insult calling humans "ugly Earthlings with their tiny heads"?
o: It is Think-Tank’s own oversized, egg-shaped head that causes him to mistake Humpty Dumpty’s picture for himself and flee in terror
Earthlings actually had larger heads than Martians
Humpty Dumpty had a tiny square head in the drawing
Noodle’s head was much larger than Think-Tank’s
e: The very balloon-like head Think-Tank boasted about became his undoing when he identified himself with the doomed Humpty Dumpty.

q: Why does the Historian emphasize that 20th-century books "illustrated, educated, punctuated, and even decorated"?
o: So that 25th-century citizens would lock all books away in museums
To highlight the enduring cultural versatility of books and contrast futuristic forgetfulness with how a single book once saved civilization
To prove that books were meant only for room decoration
To criticize the education system of Mars
e: The Historian reminds her futuristic audience of the rich intellectual and cultural role printed books played—even saving Earth itself.

q: How does Claire Boiko satirize military chain-of-command structures in the sandwich-eating episode?
o: By showing senior officers always volunteering for risky tasks themselves
By showing there was zero discipline in the Martian army
By showing foolish orders being passed down from Omega to Iota to Oop disguised as a "glorious honour" of blind obedience
By showing Sergeant Oop rebelling against his superiors
e: Superiors evade unpleasant tasks by disguising them as "honours" passed downward, exposing blind obedience and buck-passing.

q: How do the chemical vitamins function as a plot device in the play?
o: They prevent the Martians from speaking Earth’s language
They make the book pages taste sweet like sandwiches
They teleport Think-Tank down to the library
They enable the crew to suddenly read the rhymes aloud, shifting the comedy from physical blunders to absurd literal misreadings
e: The vitamins allow the crew to read the nursery rhymes aloud, driving the plot toward Think-Tank’s terrified misinterpretations.

q: What societal transformation on Mars is symbolized by Noodle succeeding Think-Tank and opening a library in Marsopolis?
o: A shift from arrogant militarism and ignorance to curiosity, literacy, humility, and peaceful diplomacy
The end of science and space exploration on Mars
A military conquest of Mars by Earth forces
Replacing all books with sandwich exports
e: Replacing a tyrant with a thoughtful leader and building a model library symbolize a shift from militaristic arrogance to shared learning and peace.

q: What subtle psychological irony explains why 25th-century Martians still cannot bring themselves to read "Mother Goose"?
o: Because the language of the book was too technical
Because the traumatic memory of how that children’s book terrified and toppled their mighty ruler lingers as a cultural taboo
Because Earthlings refused to export copies of the book
Because Noodle banned all Earth literature on Mars
e: Even centuries later as literate allies, Martians carry a lingering cultural awe and trauma over the book that defeated their supreme ruler.

q: Comparing Think-Tank’s three shifting interpretations of books (food -> ear device -> eye device), what leadership flaw is revealed?
o: He openly admits his mistakes and apologizes to his crew
He holds democratic votes among his subordinates
He steals credit for every sensible correction offered by Noodle while pretending it was his own idea all along
He conducts careful experiments before jumping to conclusions
e: Every time Noodle nudges him toward the truth, Think-Tank claims "That was my next point", exposing his habit of stealing credit.

q: Which statement best captures the central message of the play’s closing historical perspective?
o: Aggressive warfare is the only way to survive in space
Only creatures with giant heads deserve to rule the universe
Children should avoid visiting museums of ancient history
Knowledge, humility, and the power of the written word triumph over blind force and intellectual vanity
e: The play shows that literacy, humility, and wisdom ultimately triumph over military arrogance and foolish pride.

q: Select the option that identifies the error and supplies the correction for: "I can run fast when I was young."
e: Because "when I was young" refers to the past, "can" is an error and must be corrected to the past modal "could".

q: Identify the error and supply the correction in the sentence: "The ship Titanic and her fate continues to fascinate the imagination of the people."
e: The compound subject "The ship Titanic and her fate" joined by "and" is plural, so "continues" must be corrected to "continue".

q: Identify the error and correction in the headline: "Attractive packages for different Tourist destination – Mizoram, Kashmir, Kerala, Goa."
e: After "different" and preceding four named places, the singular noun "destination" is an error and must be pluralized to "destinations".

q: Select the option that identifies the error and correction in this traffic advisory: "Whoever drove a motor vehicle without a safety belt or carries passengers without seat belts will be fined."
e: For parallel tense consistency in a standing rule (matching "carries" and "will be fined"), the past verb "drove" must be corrected to "drives".

q: Identify the error and correction on this shop signboard: "For travel informations, contact the twenty-four hour help-desk."
e: "Information" is an uncountable noun and never takes a plural "-s", so "informations" must be corrected to "information".

q: Identify the error and supply the correction: "Ninety-seven percent of the Earth’s water is salty ocean water and another two percent is trapping in the Earth’s ice caps."
e: Because the water is held (passive meaning) inside ice caps, "is trapping" is wrong and must be corrected to "trapped".

q: Detect the error and supply the correction from an instruction manual: "For avoid damaging the appliance, do not immerse the electric cooker in water."
o: Error: do not | Correction: does not
e: To express purpose before the base verb "avoid", the infinitive marker "To" ("To avoid") is required instead of "For".

q: Identify and correct the error in the given line: "I prefer the chocolate pudding than the vanilla truffle any day."
e: The verb "prefer" always takes the preposition "to" rather than "than" when comparing two choices.

q: Detect the error and supply the correction: "Both his parent were proud of his remarkable achievement."
e: Both the determiner "Both" and the plural verb "were" require the plural noun "parents" instead of "parent".

q: Identify the error and supply the correction: "One must remain vigilant and response quickly to any emergency situation."
e: Following the modal "must" and parallel to "remain", a base verb is needed; the noun "response" must be corrected to the verb "respond".

q: Choose the correct verb pair to satisfy subject-verb concord: "The number of applicants ______ increased significantly, whereas a number of seats ______ still vacant."
e: "The number of..." takes a singular verb ("has"), whereas "a number of..." (meaning "many") takes a plural verb ("remain").

q: Complete the sentence with the correct correlative structure: "Not only did Mayank work hard to win the trophy, ______ helped the juniors to improve their skills."
e: The correlative conjunction "Not only" must pair with "but ... also", giving "but he also" to introduce the second clause.

q:

o: he was going in that direction
he could be going in that direction
he would be going in the direction
he is going in the direction
e: In reported speech with a past reporting verb ("offered"), "I’m going" backshifts to "he was going in that direction".

q:

o: he was running out of money

he have run out of money
e: Direct Simple Past ("ran out") backshifts to Past Perfect ("had run out of money") in reported speech.

q: Remove "too" correctly in this past-tense sentence: "The box was too heavy for the little boy to lift."
o: The box was so heavy that the little boy cannot lift it.
The box is so heavy that the little boy could not lift it.
The box was so heavy that the little boy could not lift it.
The box was very heavy for the little boy not to lift.
e: Because the main clause is in the past tense ("was"), removing "too" requires "could not" along with the implied object "it".

q: Convert the simple sentence into a compound sentence: "In spite of hard work, he failed."
o: He worked hard so he failed.
Although he worked hard, he failed.
He worked hard, but he failed.
e: Contrasting ideas in a compound sentence require the coordinating conjunction "but" ("Although" creates a complex sentence).

q: Which mistake is considered a serious formal letter etiquette pitfall when writing a Class 10 Letter to the Editor?
o: Writing "Yours obediently" or "Your’s faithfully" (with an apostrophe) instead of "Yours faithfully/truly", or using casual greetings
Including the sender’s address and date at the top
Writing a concise Subject line after the receiver’s address
Concluding with constructive suggestions within 100–120 words
e: Using "Yours obediently" (reserved for school applications) or adding an apostrophe ("Your’s") violates formal Letter to the Editor conventions.

q: Which practice must be strictly AVOIDED when writing a CBSE Class 10 Analytical Paragraph based on a chart or data table?
o: Comparing key trends, highs, and lows shown in the data
Adding personal opinions, emotional storytelling, or unsupported facts not present in the given data
Using neutral, formal, and objective language
Keeping the response to a single coherent paragraph of about 100–120 words
e: An Analytical Paragraph objectively summarizes and compares the provided data without personal bias, fictional narratives, or external claims.
